overview.title: 📖 Overview: A Master List of Every Offering's Me'ilah Timeline
overview.subtitle: Meilah 9a–9b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf first resolves the squeezing-of-blood dispute from the previous daf by reading the Zevaḥim mishna 'disjunctively' — the two disqualifications it lists apply to two different bird offerings. A sweeping new mishna then catalogs when me'ilah begins and ends for the bird burnt offering, burned bulls and goats, the burnt offering, sin/guilt/communal peace offerings, the two loaves of Shavuot, the shewbread, and meal offerings — showing that some parts (hides, remainder-meat) exit me'ilah while other parts (sacrificial portions, the handful) remain subject to it until actually burned. The Gemara then turns to two related disputes: whether ash on the altar's heap is still subject to me'ilah after the daily ash-removal, and where the money paid to atone for misuse of consecrated property is directed.

slides.title: 🩸 Resolving Yesterday's Squeezing Dispute
slides.subtitle: One mishna, read as describing two different bird offerings

steps.content: 1️⃣ Shmuel's father objects to Rav Huna: a Zevaḥim mishna says bird offerings are disqualified if pinched OR their blood squeezed with improper intent — 'squeezed' implies squeezing is essential!
2️⃣ He resolves his own objection: the mishna is taught לִצְדָדִין — disjunctively, about two different birds
3️⃣ Pinching (מְלִיקָה) applies to BOTH the bird sin offering and the bird burnt offering
4️⃣ Squeezing (מִיצּוּי) matters only for the bird BURNT offering, whose blood is never sprinkled on the altar — so squeezing intent is what counts there

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: The Gemara concludes there are simply two tanna'im who disagree, both following the school of Rabbi Yishmael, about whether missing the squeezing step invalidates a bird sin offering.

slides.subtitle: The new mishna's sweeping survey

callout.label: The pattern:
callout.text: Whatever is ultimately eaten by priests or owners exits me'ilah once permitted; whatever is entirely consumed by fire on the altar remains subject to me'ilah for its entire journey, right up to actual combustion.

slides.title: 🔥 Is the Altar's Ash Pile Still Subject to Me'ilah?
slides.subtitle: Rav vs. Rabbi Yoḥanan, after the daily removal of ashes

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: Once the mitzva of תְּרוּמַת הַדֶּשֶׁן (removing a shovelful of ash each morning) has been performed, the remaining ash pile is no longer subject to me'ilah — its mitzva is complete.

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: It remains subject to me'ilah — the verse requires priestly garments even for carrying the ash outside the camp afterward (Lev. 6:3–4), proving the ash retains its consecrated status that whole time.

lines.speaker: Agreed by both
lines.text: Before the daily removal ever happens, everyone agrees the ash pile is fully subject to me'ilah — the dispute is only about the status AFTER that mitzva is done.

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: This dispute over 'has the mitzva been completed' recurs across many areas of consecrated property — once an item has served its purpose, does sanctity linger or lapse?

slides.title: 🪨 Ember vs. Ash: Does 'Substance' Matter?
slides.subtitle: Testing both opinions against a mishna about dislodged material

nodes.content: ❓ Mishna (Zevaḥim 86a): an ember dislodged from the altar is NOT restored; implies one still ON the altar WOULD be restored
✅ For Rabbi Yoḥanan: fits perfectly — the altar's contents (even after ash removal) retain sanctity
⚡ For Rav: difficult! Rav answers: an ember is different — it still has מְשָׁשָׁא (substance, still burnable), unlike plain ash
🔄 Reversed reading: maybe ONLY an ember (with substance) is restored — plain ash, lacking substance, is NEVER subject to me'ilah, even on the altar. Now Rabbi Yoḥanan is challenged!
✅ R' Yoḥanan's answer: ash too must be restored if dislodged; the mishna mentions 'ember' specifically to teach the (bigger) novelty that even an ember with substance is NOT restored once dislodged

slides.title: 💰 Where Does the Me'ilah Payment Go?
slides.subtitle: Rav vs. Levi, harmonized with a baraita about Rabbi Shimon
slides.hebrewSource: מַה שֶׁנֶּהֱנָה – יִפְּלוּ לִנְדָבָה. וְלֵוִי אָמַר: יָבִיא דָּבָר שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ לַמִּזְבֵּחַ
slides.label: The dispute:
slides.text: For one who derives benefit from sacred-order meat before sprinkling, or from lesser-sanctity portions after sprinkling, Rav says the repaid value is allocated to communal gift offerings (nedava); Levi says one must instead bring an item entirely burned on the altar, such as incense. Baraitot support each view. A further baraita (following Rav) adds nuance: benefiting from money set aside for a sin/guilt offering before it was sacrificed requires adding to the fund and buying a costlier animal; after the offering was already brought, the money goes to the Dead Sea (for a sin offering, per Rabbi Shimon's rule that an atoned-for sin offering is left to die) or to communal gifts (for a guilt offering, which has no such rule).

summary.principle: Every category of offering has its own precise window for me'ilah, ending only when the item is truly consumed — by priests, by fire, or by placement outside the sacred system — and even the ash and coals on the altar, and the money used to atone for misuse, follow parallel rules about when sanctity truly lapses.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the apparent conflict between Rav Huna's ruling and the Zevaḥim mishna that mentions 'squeezed out their blood'?
o: By rejecting the Zevaḥim mishna entirely
By reading the mishna disjunctively: pinching applies to both bird offerings, but squeezing the blood is only relevant to the bird burnt offering
By saying squeezing is always required for both offerings
By claiming the mishna is discussing animal offerings, not birds
quiz.e: Shmuel's father resolves his own objection by explaining the mishna teaches its two clauses about two different offerings — pinching for both, squeezing specifically for the bird burnt offering.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna's survey, what determines when a given part of an offering exits me'ilah?
o: The day of the week it was offered
Whether that part is ultimately eaten (by priests or owners) or entirely consumed by fire on the altar
The species of animal used
Nothing — all offerings have identical me'ilah timelines
quiz.e: Parts destined to be eaten (hides, meat, remainder) exit me'ilah once permitted for consumption; parts entirely burned on the altar (sacrificial portions, the handful) remain subject to me'ilah until actually consumed by fire.

quiz.q: What is the core dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan regarding the ash pile on the altar?
o: Whether the ash may be touched by non-priests
Whether the ash remains subject to me'ilah after the daily removal (terumat hadeshen) mitzva has been performed
Whether ash can ever become impure
Whether the altar itself is subject to me'ilah
quiz.e: Both agree the ash is subject to me'ilah before the daily removal; they disagree about afterward — Rav says the mitzva is complete and me'ilah ends, Rabbi Yoḥanan says sanctity persists (proven from the requirement of priestly garments even for the later removal outside the camp).

quiz.q: How does Rav explain the mishna's ruling that a dislodged ember must be restored to the altar, given his own opinion that ash is not subject to me'ilah after removal?
o: He rejects the mishna as inauthentic
He distinguishes an ember, which still has 'substance' (meshasha) and remains burnable, from plain ash which lacks it
He says embers are never placed on the altar
He says the mishna refers only to bird offerings
quiz.e: Rav explains that an ember, unlike ash, retains substance and burnability, which is why it must be restored to the altar even according to his view that plain ash loses its sanctity.

quiz.q: According to Levi's opinion, what must one bring to atone for deriving benefit from sacred-order meat before sprinkling, or lesser-sanctity portions after sprinkling?
o: Nothing — no atonement is required
The value must be used to purchase an item entirely consumed on the altar, such as incense
The value must be given directly to the poor
A new sin offering must be brought
quiz.e: Levi holds that the repaid value for such misuse must fund something that is entirely burned on the altar (like incense), matching the nature of what was misused; Rav instead directs it to communal gift offerings.
